paras: On the night of August 23, 1903, several men in St. Paul, Minnesota, chased an unidentified Black man after Mary M. Hagan fired her revolver at him at the corner of Eighth and Sibley streets, saying he had grabbed her arm. The man escaped, and the Saint Paul Globe, the only paper found to report the incident, wrote that the pursuers "would have used summary methods had they overtaken him."

Hagan ran the St. Paul Messenger and Express company with her brother Percy and worked at the messenger office until after 11 o'clock each night. According to her, a Black man had repeatedly followed her and "frightened her" as she walked home alone, so she began carrying a revolver.

At about 11:30 p.m., Hagan said, the man grabbed her by the arm at Eighth and Sibley, and she fired three times. She did not think she hit him, though she saw him hold a handkerchief to the side of his face as he ran.
The shots drew a crowd, and "great excitement prevailed." Several men ran after him in the direction he had taken but did not catch him.

No arrest or identification of the man appears in the coverage. In April 1904, reporting Hagan's arrest for shooting Joseph Clinton, the Globe recalled that a "negro" had seized her arm near Eighth and Sibley "seven months ago" and tried to throw her down, and that he escaped.

The Globe ran the story under the headline "SHE FIRES THRICE AND NEGRO FLEES," with a deck praising Hagan's "Heroic Measures." Resting on Hagan's account, it called the man only an "unknown colored man" and "the negro" and noted the pursuers' "summary methods" without comment. Seven months later the same paper retold the episode to show that her revolver had "protected her" before, calling her "the brave one-armed girl."

The two Globe accounts differ: the 1903 report quotes Hagan as firing three shots after he grabbed her arm, while the 1904 retelling gives two shots and adds that he tried to throw her down; the earlier report is the closer source.

reader.title: Pursuit of an unidentified Black man after the Hagan shooting, St. Paul (1903)
bases: The only report describes several men from a gathering crowd chasing an unidentified Black man who fled after being accused of grabbing a woman, saying they 'would have used summary methods' had they caught him; he was not caught and no one was harmed by the pursuers (A1).

No one was killed: several men pursued the man under an accusation of assaulting a white woman, and the Globe's phrase 'would have used summary methods' implies an intent to punish him, but he escaped (A1, A2). At most this was a threatened or attempted lynching.

The only contemporary account is the Saint Paul Globe of August 24, 1903, resting on Hagan's own statement (A1); the Globe's 1904 retrospective is the same paper recalling the incident, not an independent report (A2).

accounts.label: Hagan's statement (Saint Paul Globe, 1903)
accounts.gist: The man had followed her home on several nights; when he grabbed her arm she fired three times; he ran off holding a handkerchief to his face.

accounts.label: Saint Paul Globe retrospective (1904)
accounts.gist: Seven months earlier a 'negro' had seized her arm near Eighth and Sibley and tried to throw her down; she fired two shots and he escaped.

framing.detail: The Globe headlined 'SHE FIRES THRICE AND NEGRO FLEES', praised her 'Heroic Measures', and reported that the pursuers 'would have used summary methods' without criticism.
In 1904 the Globe recalled the incident as proof that her revolver 'protected her' and cast her as 'the brave one-armed girl'.

conflicts.note: The contemporary report quoting Hagan (A1) is the better evidence; A2 is a retrospective seven months later.

record_check.dossier: A chase by several men who would have used 'summary methods'; no one was caught or killed. Better coded as a mob assault (threatened lynching) than a lynching.
Threatened: the men ran after him but never overtook him; the intent is the paper's inference, and no act of violence by the pursuers is reported.
